newsitem.title: USA: BASEBALL-BREWERS SIGN JULIO FRANCO FOR REST OF SEASON.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-BREWERS SIGN JULIO FRANCO FOR REST OF SEASON.

text.p: Infielder Julio Franco, released less than two weeks ago by the Cleveland Indians, was signed Wednesday for the remainder of the season by the Milwaukee Brewers, who hope the one-time batting champion can help them catch his former team.
The 35-year-old Franco was hitting .284 with three homers and 25 RBI when the Indians designated him for assignment on August 1, one day after swinging deals for pitchers Jeff Juden and John Smiley.
Franco began the season as Cleveland's starting second baseman but struggled defensively and was unseated by Tony Fernandez.
Franco, who plays first base, second base or designated hitter, joins his fifth major-league team. He has batted no lower than .273 in any full season in his 14-year career.
"Julio brings an experienced presence to our club," Brewers vice president Sal Bando said. "His offensive abilities are going to be a big plus for us down the stretch."

Scheduled to earn $2.5 million this year, Franco cleared waivers Wednesday. According to the Cleveland Plain-Dealer, the Brewers will pay him a pro-rated minimum of $150,000 while the Indians pick up the rest.

The Brewers (57-60) stood third in the American League Central Division, 3 1/2 games behind the first-place Indians after Cleveland won the first game of a doubleheader with the Detroit Tigers Wednesday. Milwuakee was not playing Wednesday.
Despite being 12th in the A.L. in homers with no .300 hitters, the Brewers are bidding for their first postseason berth in 15 years.
Franco has played with Philadelphia, Cleveland, Texas and the Chicago White Sox. He spent 1995 in Japan and has major-league totals of 134 homers, 937 RBI and a .303 average.

During a five-year stint with Texas beginning in 1989, Franco was named to the A.L. All-Star team three times, winning the game's Most Valuable Player award in 1990. In 1991, he led the A.L. with a .341 average.
Franco's best season may have been the strike-shortened campaign of 1994, when he hit .318 with career highs of 20 homers and 98 RBI for the White Sox.
